text: I think remote work is very good in terms of flexibility, no commute, no shared spaces with other people, and no distraction. And yet, for some people, especially, it can cause loneliness. And loneliness is very, very complicated. Being alone is not the same as loneliness. Loneliness is having a gap between the social connection that you want and the social connection that you actually get. So remote work can amplify that and very easy to get lonely. The problem is that we are very social people and loneliness, chronic loneliness, is associated with many diseases, from depression and anxiety to cardiovascular problems, sleep problems, cognitive decline. So remote work, why does it cause loneliness? First of all, remote work eliminates ambient sociality. In a regular office, a lot of social interaction is very incidental. You talk with somebody in the coffee room. You talk with somebody while going to a meeting. You overhear a joke or you ask a question. Those little things are very important because they create weak ties that make you feel part of something and they are so easy. And in remote work, everything is very intentional. You have to call somebody or you have to message or have a meeting and a meeting needs an agenda. So it's very easy to go days without very casual interactions. And that can feel very lonely, even if you have your calendar full. Second, remote work makes interactions very narrow. On video call, you only see words and some facial expression. And sometimes, those things are very performative or transactional. You don't have peripheral awareness, you don't have side conversations, you don't have people coming over to your desk, you don't have shared spaces. So it's very easy to feel that you're doing something very transactional, very status oriented, very task oriented and not relationship oriented. Zoom fatigue, people complain about that a lot. And then you have text chat that is very efficient but it can be very ambiguous, very hard to read the tone. So sometimes people feel that they're not really able to get to know each other. And they end up feeling more and more lonely, even though they talk to people all day, because those interactions don't satisfy. Sometimes, it even backfires and people become introverted. Third, remote work removes boundaries, so it removes time for social interaction. People start earlier, people work later. They answer messages at night. Their home becomes their office. And their office doesn't really end. So it's very easy to feel too exhausted to meet somebody, to go to a club, to see somebody. At the same time, you don't have the social support of colleagues that you had before. You can complain to them, you can celebrate things with them. So the effects are doubled. Not only you have more stress that comes from working, but also you don't have someone to process that stress with. And then, remote work impacts people in a very asymmetric way. Some people are in the industry for a very long time and they have a very strong network. They have a partner, they have a very active social life. They can thrive in remote work. Some other people, early career people, new hires, people that came to another country, they live alone, they are more extroverted, they have less social networks, they will suffer a lot more. New hires miss out a lot on mentorship and on informal learning that happens in offices. People that live alone may go a whole day without talking to someone in person. Or people that are parents, they feel lonely in a different way. They are surrounded by people but they don't have peers. So it's very context dependent. And remote work can also help, for example, people that are introverted, people that have some disability, people that feel discriminated against in office. So remote work is a life saver for them. Now, the very good news is that loneliness is not a given in remote work. And you can improve it a lot. And this is something that companies should really design. They should create opportunities for very casual interactions. Virtual coffees, no agenda. Mentorship programs, employee resource groups, one on ones that really address well-being, not just performance. Some occasional in-person meetups. And managers should really model the boundaries, not send messages at night, have space for non-work interactions. Hybrid is also very good because it preserves some in-person interactions. It doesn't mean that people will be friends, but it creates social infrastructure. For individuals, what can they do? They can schedule social interaction as they schedule meetings. They can go to coworking spaces, clubs, classes, etc. They can create rituals. I do walks with a neighbor, I have lunch with my friends. I have a game night every week online, and so on. They can define a very clear end to workday. They can have a very specific space at home for work. Some people, therapy and groups can really help, especially when loneliness becomes chronic and is associated with anxiety or depression. And we have to really accept that loneliness is a signal, not a judgement. In conclusion, remote work and loneliness are connected because it removes the incidental, the embodied, the very structured social interactions that we had before. And it makes interactions very intentional, very narrow and easy to postpone. And the risk is higher for people that have less social networks outside of work, for early career people. But remote work is not the enemy. We have to design it better, we have to have boundaries, we have to have rituals, we have to have mentorship and some in-person. And that's how we can really make remote work work.
